title: The Carpenter's Shop and the Crypt: Millais, the Brotherhood, and the Long Perthshire Autumn
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Island Child and the Youngest Student

stops.name: Southampton, the second son
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: In a lodging at Southampton a second son is born to John William Millais and his wife Emily Mary, born Evermy, a woman who has buried one husband already and carries a name from that first marriage into this one. The father's people are Jersey people, gentry of the Channel Islands with land at Saint Ouen, and the child is entered on the English mainland only by the accident of where the household happens to be living. They name him John Everett. Within a short time the family is back across the water, and the boy's first country is an island that answers to two crowns.
suggested_refs: The Southampton birth entry of 8 June 1829

stops.name: St Helier, the island childhood
stops.date_confidence: range; the source gives no exact years for the Jersey period
stops.campa: The boy grows up on Jersey, his father's ancestral island, where the family name is old and the sea is the boundary of everything. He draws before he writes properly. There is no drawing master on the island and no gallery in it, and nothing he learns here is formal; what he has is a coast and the hours to look at it. The attachment holds for the rest of his life: sixty years on, when Queen Victoria makes him a baronet, the patent will name him of Saint Ouen in the island of Jersey as well as of Kensington in London.
suggested_refs: The Millais lands at Saint Ouen, Jersey, named in the 1885 baronetcy patent

stops.name: Dinan, the drawing noticed
stops.date_confidence: approximate; the source gives no dates for the Brittany years
stops.campa: The family crosses to Brittany and settles for several years at Dinan above the Rance, a walled town of timber houses and garrison officers. Here the boy's drawing stops being a household amusement and becomes a fact that other adults remark on. The account the family gives afterwards is of officers passing his sketches from hand to hand, and of a mother who decides on that evidence that the child is to be a painter and that London is where painters are made. No document survives from the Breton years; the story reaches the atlas through the son's Life and Letters, sixty years later.
suggested_refs: The old town of Dinan above the Rance, the family's Breton residence

stops.name: Bloomsbury, the drilling at Sass's academy
stops.date_confidence: attested year of the family's arrival in London; the exact date of entry to the academy is not recorded in the sources consulted
stops.campa: The family moves to London for the sake of the boy alone. At No. 6 Charlotte Street, at the corner of Streatham Street in Bloomsbury, Henry Sass runs the preparatory academy that feeds the Royal Academy Schools: plaster casts, outline drawing, the antique copied until the hand obeys without argument. Millais is nine when he enters it. Sass drills his pupils for one examination and one only, and the boy who sits it will do so younger than any candidate the Academy has yet accepted.
suggested_refs: Henry Sass's academy, No. 6 Charlotte Street at the corner of Streatham Street, Bloomsbury
sources: Tate, biography of John Everett Millais

stops.name: Trafalgar Square, the youngest student admitted
stops.date_confidence: attested year; month and day not given by the source
stops.campa: The Royal Academy keeps its schools in the east wing of the National Gallery on Trafalgar Square, having left Somerset House three years before and not yet moved to Burlington House. Into these rooms, at eleven years old, walks the youngest student the institution has ever admitted. He takes its silver medal at that age and its gold at seventeen. In the same rooms he meets a young man named William Holman Hunt and another named Dante Gabriel Rossetti, the son of an Italian exile, and the three of them find each other useful.
suggested_refs: The Royal Academy Schools in the east wing of the National Gallery, occupied 1837 to 1868

stops.name: Keston, the Kentish sketching ground
stops.date_confidence: approximate; the source dates these expeditions only to his youth
stops.campa: On free days the students go out of London into Kent, to Keston and to Hayes a mile or two north of it, with paint boxes and no studio. What the Academy teaches indoors is the antique cast; what the Kentish commons teach is that leaves have edges, and that light on chalk is not the same colour as light on water. Millais is sketching these fields years before anybody in England speaks of painting every touch from Nature. The habit of working out of doors, in front of the thing itself, is fixed before there is a doctrine to justify it.
suggested_refs: The commons at Keston and Hayes, Kent, named among his youthful sketching grounds

stops.name: Gower Street, Pizarro seizing the Inca
stops.date_confidence: attested year
stops.campa: At seventeen he exhibits Pizarro Seizing the Inca of Peru, a full history painting in the grand manner the Academy rewards: conquistadors, plunder, a captive king, everything arranged as the schools instruct that it should be arranged. It is a prodigy's picture and it is entirely orthodox. Two years later he will help write a programme against exactly this kind of composition. The Millais family is by now living at 83 Gower Street, and the son's studio is a room in his parents' house.
suggested_refs: Pizarro Seizing the Inca of Peru (1846), Victoria and Albert Museum

stops.name: 83 Gower Street, the Brotherhood founded
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the month is not given by the source, and one reading of the research pool dated the founding to September 1847
stops.campa: In his parents' house on Gower Street three young men bind themselves into a Brotherhood: Millais, Holman Hunt, Rossetti, with four more added to make seven. They will sign their canvases PRB and tell nobody what the letters stand for. Their programme is to go behind Raphael to the painters who worked before him, and to paint what they see instead of what the schools prescribe. In the same year, at Exeter College in Oxford, two undergraduates named William Morris and Edward Jones form a brotherhood of their own and turn from the Church toward Art. Neither pair knows the other exists.
stops.quote: Now, look here, this is what the Pre-Raphaelite clique should follow.
stops.quote_source: Millais at the meeting where the terms of the Brotherhood were settled, in J. G. Millais, The Life and Letters of Sir John Everett Millais (1899), vol. 1, p. 51
suggested_refs: 83 Gower Street, Bloomsbury, the Millais family house where the PRB was founded
sources: J. G. Millais, Life and Letters, vol. 1, p. 51

stops.name: Gower Street, Christ in the House of His Parents
stops.date_confidence: the source dates the picture 1849 to 1850
stops.campa: In the room at Gower Street he paints a carpenter's shop: shavings on the floor, a boy with a cut hand, a mother kneeling on the boards, and Joseph's forearms those of a working joiner because a working joiner sat for them. The doctrine is the Nazarene doctrine forty years on, the quattrocento chosen over Raphael, which Johann Friedrich Overbeck and Franz Pforr carried over the Alps to Rome; these Londoners reach it without leaving Bloomsbury. Nobody in England has seen the Holy Family painted as poor people before.
stops.quote: We can hardly imagine anything more ugly, graceless, and unpleasant than Mr. Millais' picture of 'Christ in the Carpenter's Shop.' Such a collection of splay feet, puffed joints, and misshapen limbs was assuredly never before made within so small a compass.
stops.quote_source: Blackwood's Magazine, 1850, quoted in J. G. Millais, Life and Letters, vol. 1, p. 75
suggested_refs: Christ in the House of His Parents (1849-50), Tate
The Nazarene Lukasbund of Overbeck and Pforr, founded Vienna 1809
sources: J. G. Millais, Life and Letters, vol. 1, p. 75

stops.name: London, Household Words answers the picture
stops.date_confidence: attested date of the Household Words article
stops.campa: The picture goes up at the Academy and the press turns on it as on an offence rather than a failure. The Times calls it revolting. Blackwood's counts its splay feet and its misshapen limbs. Charles Dickens gives it a leading article in his own weekly and instructs his readers to prepare themselves for the lowest depths. Millais is twenty-one and the most abused painter in London. Fourteen years later Dickens will write to him as a friend and mean it, and the friendship will outlast the review by decades.
stops.quote: the lowest depths of what is mean, odious, repulsive, and revolting
stops.quote_source: Charles Dickens, 'Old Lamps for New Ones,' Household Words, 15 June 1850; the 1899 biography prints the four words in the order revolting and repulsive
suggested_refs: 'Old Lamps for New Ones,' Household Words, 15 June 1850
sources: Dickens Journals Online, Household Words vol. I, p. 265
J. G. Millais, Life and Letters, vol. 1, pp. 75-76

stops.name: London, Ruskin takes up arms
stops.date_confidence: the biography dates Ruskin's public defence to 1851; the month is inferred from the Academy exhibition season
stops.campa: John Ruskin is thirty-two, the critic who has told a generation to go to Nature rejecting nothing and selecting nothing, and he sees that these young men have taken him at his word. He writes to The Times on their behalf, then in Modern Painters, then from a lecture platform in Edinburgh. Nobody has asked him for any of it. The painters he is defending are the ones the London papers have spent a year calling disgusting. Two years later the same critic will invite Millais to Scotland to paint his portrait against a rock, and will bring his wife with him.
stops.quote: the admirable, though strange pictures of Mr. Millais and Mr. Holman Hunt... they are endeavouring to paint, with the highest possible degree of completion, what they see in Nature, without reference to conventional or established rules.
stops.quote_source: John Ruskin, Modern Painters, quoted in J. G. Millais, Life and Letters, vol. 1, pp. 111-112
suggested_refs: Ruskin's 1851 letters to The Times in defence of the Pre-Raphaelites
sources: J. G. Millais, Life and Letters, vol. 1, pp. 111-112

stops.name: Old Malden, five months on the Hogsmill
stops.date_confidence: the source dates the campaign to 1851 and gives its length as five months, without start and end dates
stops.campa: On the Hogsmill River at Old Malden, in a field called Six Acre Meadow beside Church Road, he sets up for five months: eleven hours a day, six days a week, inside a hut of hurdles thatched with straw against the wind. Every willow, every loosestrife and forget-me-not on that bank goes onto the canvas at the size and in the place the bank itself puts them. The drowning girl is not there yet. He paints the water first, and the water will have to wait through a winter for its Ophelia.
suggested_refs: Six Acre Meadow, Church Road, Old Malden, identified as the Ophelia site by the research of Barbara Webb

stops.name: Kingston, the flies of Surrey
stops.date_confidence: the letter is dated to 1851 by the biography; month and day are not given
stops.campa: He lodges at Kingston to be near the river, and writes from there to Mrs. Combe about the conditions of the work. Not the loneliness and not the hours: the insects. Holman Hunt is at work about four miles off on a picture of his own, the two of them staked out in Surrey fields like surveyors. Painting every touch from Nature turns out to mean sitting in one place from morning until the light goes, in whatever weather the month provides, and being bitten throughout.
stops.quote: My martyrdom is more trying than any I have hitherto experienced. The flies of Surrey are more muscular, and have a still greater propensity for probing human flesh.
stops.quote_source: Millais to Mrs. Combe from Kingston, 1851, in J. G. Millais, Life and Letters, vol. 1, p. 119 (Archive scan lifelettersofsir01milluoft; the scan lifelettersofsir01mill misreads flies as tiles)
suggested_refs: The 1851 Kingston letters to Mrs. Combe, printed in Life and Letters, vol. 1
sources: J. G. Millais, Life and Letters, vol. 1, p. 119

stops.name: Gower Street, Elizabeth Siddal in the bath
stops.date_confidence: the source dates the picture 1851 to 1852; the sittings are not separately dated
stops.campa: Back in the studio the water is a bathtub and the model is Elizabeth Siddal, lying full length in an old dress with oil lamps under the tub to keep the water warm. One afternoon the lamps go out and neither painter nor sitter notices; she holds the pose in cold water until the light fails, takes a severe cold from it, and her father sends Millais a demand for fifty pounds of doctor's bills. The face that comes out of that tub becomes the drowned woman of England, the image the Ophelia of Paul Barbier's Hamlet is still measured against.
suggested_refs: Ophelia (1851-52), Tate
Barbier and Carre's Hamlet (1868), the Ophelia the atlas measures against this canvas

stops.name: Glen Finglas, the rock and the portrait
stops.date_confidence: the sources date the expedition to the summer of 1853; the month is inferred
stops.campa: In the Trossachs the party settles to a commission: Ruskin standing on the gneiss beside a waterfall in Glen Finglas, the rock to be painted first, stone by stone, with the man put in afterwards. The rock takes months. Millais paints it as the doctrine requires, every fracture in its own place, while the critic watches and the critic's wife, Euphemia Gray, sits nearby. By the time the canvas is finished the sitter has his portrait, the painter has fallen in love with the sitter's wife, and none of the three of them says so aloud.
suggested_refs: John Ruskin (1853-54), Ashmolean Museum, the Glenfinlas portrait

stops.name: Brig o' Turk, the cottage summer
stops.date_confidence: the sources place the lodging in the summer of 1853; the month is inferred
stops.campa: The lodging is a cottage near the hamlet of Brig o' Turk, where the three of them eat at one table through a Highland summer and autumn. Millais draws Effie repeatedly: in the schoolroom, at the waterfall, her hair down. One sketch is titled The Waterfall, or Effie at Glenfinlas. Ruskin writes. The rain comes down on the Trossachs. The three of them leave letters that agree on nothing except that something happened, and the arguing has gone on since, in biographies, in a BBC serial, in a film.
suggested_refs: The Waterfall, or Effie at Glenfinlas, drawn at Brig o' Turk in 1853

stops.name: Trafalgar Square, elected associate
stops.date_confidence: attested year; the month is not given by the source
stops.campa: At twenty-four he is elected an associate of the Royal Academy, five years after helping to found a secret society against most of what it stands for. Holman Hunt notes the defection. Rossetti writes that the Brotherhood is dissolved. In Edinburgh that same autumn Ruskin stands before a lecture audience and tells them that the Pre-Raphaelites are young and that the war is still in front of them, not knowing how completely the war in front of this one will be domestic, nor that his own wife is at the centre of it.
stops.quote: I thank God that the Pre-Raphaelites are young, and that strength is still with them, and life, with all the war of it, still in front of them.
stops.quote_source: John Ruskin, Lectures on Architecture and Painting, Edinburgh, November 1853, quoted in J. G. Millais, Life and Letters, vol. 1, p. 112
suggested_refs: Ruskin's Edinburgh lectures of November 1853
sources: J. G. Millais, Life and Letters, vol. 1, p. 112

stops.name: Winchelsea, the double rainbow
stops.date_confidence: the source dates the picture 1854 to 1856; the year given here is the opening of that range
stops.campa: On the hill at Winchelsea, above the Sussex levels, he paints the country behind The Blind Girl: a double rainbow standing over wet fields, cattle, rooks, a town on its ridge, all of it seen and none of it invented. The blind girl herself will feel the sun on her face and the concertina under her hands and never see the arch the whole picture is arranged around. He is at work on it across the years in which Effie Ruskin's marriage is taken through the courts and annulled.
suggested_refs: The Blind Girl (1854-56), Birmingham Museum and Art Gallery
sources: Wikipedia, List of paintings by John Everett Millais

stops.name: Bowerswell, the wedding at Kinnoull
stops.date_confidence: the source attests the year 1855 only; the date of 3 July and the venue of Bowerswell come from standard biography and are reconstruction
stops.campa: At Bowerswell, on the high ground of Kinnoull above the Tay, Effie Gray marries John Everett Millais. It is the same house in which she married John Ruskin seven years before. That marriage has been annulled and she has come home to Perth to wait out the scandal; the Queen will not receive her for decades yet. Millais gains a wife, eight children in the end, and a country he will return to every autumn for the rest of his working life. Of the ceremony itself the sources consulted give a year and nothing more.
suggested_refs: Bowerswell House, Kinnoull, Perth, where Effie Gray married twice

stops.name: Annat Lodge, the burning of the leaves
stops.date_confidence: the source dates the residence from 1855; the month is inferred from the wedding
stops.campa: The couple sets up at Annat Lodge, a house at Kinnoull within sight of the one where the wedding was held. In its garden, at the hour when the light turns blue, four girls heap fallen leaves and burn them, and Millais paints Autumn Leaves. There is no text behind the picture and no incident in it, nothing the viewer is meant to recognise: smoke, children, a season ending. He will keep coming back to this county for forty years, and a great deal of what he paints from here on is ground he can walk to from a rented house.
suggested_refs: Autumn Leaves (1856), Manchester Art Gallery, painted in the Annat Lodge garden

stops.name: Trafalgar Square, the hanging of 1856
stops.date_confidence: attested date of the letter
stops.campa: The Academy hangs him badly again and he writes to his wife about it in the language of a man who has forgiven nothing. He is an associate of the body he is abusing, will be a full member of it within seven years, and will hold its chair within forty; none of that is visible from inside the year 1856. What is visible is a wall of pictures with his own placed where the light does not reach them, and the settled suspicion that applause from this quarter would be a worse sign than neglect.
stops.quote: I never saw anything more shameless than the treatment by the R.A. of my work. Every year it is the same. The surest sign of a young man's work being worthless is generosity and applause from the Academy!
stops.quote_source: Millais to his wife, 8 May 1856, in J. G. Millais, Life and Letters, vol. 1, p. 300
suggested_refs: The Royal Academy summer exhibition of 1856 in the National Gallery east wing
sources: J. G. Millais, Life and Letters, vol. 1, p. 300

stops.name: Kinnoull, the gravestones of The Vale of Rest
stops.date_confidence: the source dates the picture 1858 to 1859
stops.campa: In the old churchyard at Kinnoull he paints gravestones for The Vale of Rest: two nuns digging a grave in the last of the light, a coffin-shaped cloud crossing the sky behind them. The picture is made in the first years of his marriage, in the parish where he was married, from stones he can walk to from the house. Nobody commissions it and nobody asks for it. Effie will lie in this same ground in the end, under a marker she shares with their son George, who dies at twenty-one.
suggested_refs: The Vale of Rest (1858-59), Tate; the gravestones painted at Kinnoull old churchyard

stops.name: 7 Cromwell Place, the household in Kensington
stops.date_confidence: attested year; month and day not given by the source
stops.campa: The family moves to 7 Cromwell Place in South Kensington, a large house for a household that will run to eight children, and Millais settles into the career the Academy offers a man who can paint. In London that same season Morris, Marshall, Faulkner and Co. is a year old, founded at Red Lion Square by Rossetti, Edward Burne-Jones, Ford Madox Brown and William Morris, with Jane Morris and her sister at the embroidery frames. That half of the Pre-Raphaelite inheritance is going into looms, glass and workshops. Millais's is going into portrait commissions and the house they are painted in.
suggested_refs: 7 Cromwell Place, South Kensington, the family's London house from 1862

stops.name: Trafalgar Square, full Academician
stops.date_confidence: attested year; month and day not given by the source
stops.campa: He is elected a full Royal Academician at thirty-four, in the rooms behind the National Gallery portico where he entered the schools as a child of eleven. Twenty-three years separate the two doors. The initials PRB have not appeared on his canvases for a decade, and the man The Times called revolting in 1850 now sets his own price for a portrait and raises it year on year. Nothing in the Academy's gift is withheld from him now except the chair at its head, and other men hold that for another thirty-three years.
suggested_refs: The Royal Academy diploma works, deposited on election as Academician

stops.name: Gad's Hill Place, Dickens writes his thanks
stops.date_confidence: attested date of the letter
stops.campa: From his house on the Rochester road Charles Dickens writes to thank Millais. The illustrator John Leech is dead and has left a family without money, and Millais has been working the committees and the correspondence to get them a Civil List pension. Fourteen years earlier this same correspondent told the readers of Household Words to prepare for the lowest depths of what is mean and revolting, meaning a picture of a carpenter's shop. Neither man mentions it. Dickens signs himself a friend.
stops.quote: You are a generous and true friend to Mrs. Leech.
stops.quote_source: Charles Dickens to Millais, 18 December 1864, in J. G. Millais, Life and Letters, vol. 1, p. 275
suggested_refs: Gad's Hill Place, Higham-by-Rochester, Dickens's house from 1856
sources: J. G. Millais, Life and Letters, vol. 1, p. 275

stops.name: Perth, the seventh child
stops.date_confidence: attested date and town; the pin at Bowerswell is inferred, the source naming only Perth
stops.campa: At Perth, in the country his wife came from, the seventh of the eight children is born and named John Guille Millais. He is the fourth son, and he will grow into a naturalist and a hunter. In 1899 he publishes the two volumes of his father's life and letters, and that book becomes the record: almost every sentence anyone quotes of Millais's speech passes through this son's hand. He takes down the father's fury at bad hangings, the father's flat denial of Rossetti's influence, and the family's own account of the founding at Gower Street.
suggested_refs: J. G. Millais, The Life and Letters of Sir John Everett Millais (Methuen, 1899), 2 vols.

stops.name: Kinnoull, the west window given
stops.date_confidence: attested year of the donation; the parable illustrations on which the designs are based date from 1864
stops.campa: Effie's father gives the west window of Kinnoull church, and the glass is made to Millais's designs, worked up from the parables he drew six years earlier for the wood engravers. Sowers, virgins with lamps, a son coming home: subjects that went out through the printed page come back as coloured light in a Perthshire parish. The painter denounced for showing the Holy Family as poor working people now furnishes a Scottish parish church with its window. Gray pays for the glass and his son-in-law draws it; outside the wall is the ground where Gray's daughter will be buried.
suggested_refs: The Millais west window, Kinnoull Parish Church, donated 1870
The Parables of Our Lord, illustrated by Millais and engraved by the Dalziel brothers, 1864

segments.name: Chill October and the Perthshire Autumns

stops.name: Kinfauns, every touch from Nature
stops.date_confidence: attested year; the month is inferred from the subject and title
stops.campa: On a backwater of the Tay just below Kinfauns, within sight of the Perth to Dundee road, he sets a canvas on the bank and paints Chill October: reeds, flood water, a wind coming across, no figure, no incident, no story to be told. On the stretcher he writes that he made no sketch for it, and painted every touch from Nature on the canvas itself. It is his first large Scottish landscape, and it opens the last twenty-five years of his working life, which will be spent in great part out of doors in this county.
stops.quote: I made no sketch for it, but painted every touch from Nature, on the canvas itself.
stops.quote_source: Millais's note on the stretcher of Chill October, quoted in Wikipedia, Chill October
suggested_refs: Chill October (1870), painted at a backwater of the Tay below Kinfauns

stops.name: Budleigh Salterton, the boyhood of Raleigh
stops.date_confidence: attested year of painting; the picture is exhibited at the Royal Academy in 1871
stops.campa: On the sea wall at Budleigh Salterton he sets two boys on the shingle beside an old sailor whose arm points out over the water. His own sons Everett and George sit for the boys. The picture is The Boyhood of Raleigh, and it goes to the Academy the following year and becomes a schoolroom image of England for a century: an empire explained as a story told to children by a man with a tarred hand. The Devon light in it was painted on the spot, on the coast where the boy Raleigh is supposed to have listened.
suggested_refs: The Boyhood of Raleigh (1870), Tate, painted at Budleigh Salterton

stops.name: Dunkeld, the rented autumns
stops.date_confidence: the source gives the pattern as annual from 1870 to 1892; the year and month here stand for the whole series
stops.campa: From August into late autumn, every year for more than twenty years, he rents a large house near Dunkeld or neighbouring Birnam and moves the household north. The days go to shooting and to salmon; the pictures are made in the same hours and the same weather, canvases carried out to the riverbank and worked until the light fails. He does this from 1870 until 1892 without missing a year. The London portrait practice pays for the season, and the landscapes come back south in the luggage.
suggested_refs: The rented houses of Dunkeld and Birnam, occupied every autumn from 1870 to 1892

stops.name: Stobhall, the salmon beat
stops.date_confidence: traditional; no source consulted this pass attests the Stobhall fishing, and the year stands for the Perthshire decades generally
stops.campa: Downstream from Murthly the Tay runs past Stobhall, and the salmon beat there is named again and again in accounts of Millais's sporting life. He fishes it, the tradition holds, through the Perthshire seasons of his last two decades. The atlas carries the tradition and not a document. The pattern around it is attested well enough: an autumn spent on this river, rod and gun and easel carried out of the house together, the same water that gave him Chill October giving him his sport.
suggested_refs: The Stobhall beat of the River Tay, north of Perth
sources: General Millais biography, unverified this pass

stops.name: Murthly, the first snow scene
stops.date_confidence: attested year; the month is inferred from the subject
stops.campa: In the woods around Murthly Castle he paints his first full snow scene, Christmas Eve: bare trees, a house across white ground, the winter dusk of a Perthshire estate. He is fifty-eight. The ground is the ground of nearly twenty seasons of sport and it has become the subject rather than the setting. Nothing in the picture is there to be denounced or defended. It is snow on an estate he has shot over for twenty seasons, put down by a man who has had a long time to look at it.
suggested_refs: Christmas Eve (1887), a view toward Murthly Castle, Perthshire

stops.name: Cromwell Place, The North-West Passage
stops.date_confidence: attested year
stops.campa: He paints The North-West Passage: an old sea captain in his chair, a young woman reading to him from a log book, charts on the table and a flag on the wall behind. The gloss attached to the title runs that it might be done, and that England ought to do it. The picture sells as nothing of his has sold before and is engraved into thousands of parlours. Twenty-four years separate it from the carpenter's shop that The Times called revolting, and the same hand made both of them.
suggested_refs: The North-West Passage (1874), Tate
Millais's Victory O Lord! (1871), cited elsewhere in the atlas as a visual reference for Moses at Rephidim

stops.name: 2 Palace Gate, the house he builds
stops.date_confidence: the source gives occupation from 1875; the building dates are not specified
stops.campa: He builds a house at Palace Gate in Kensington to his own requirements, with a studio large enough for the biggest canvases and a staircase built for the traffic of sitters. It costs a fortune, and the fortune is there. The boy drilled at Sass's academy, who walked into the schools at eleven, now lives in a house designed around his working day. He will die in it twenty-one years later, in the year he is elected President, and the name of the street will be written into his baronetcy.
suggested_refs: 2 Palace Gate, Kensington, built for Millais and occupied from 1875

stops.name: Palace Gate, the Princes and Cherry Ripe
stops.date_confidence: The Princes in the Tower is dated 1878 and Cherry Ripe 1879; the stop takes the earlier year
stops.campa: In the Palace Gate studio he paints two children on a stair in the Tower of London, holding hands, waiting for what every English schoolchild knows is coming; and then a small girl in a mob cap seated in a wood with her hands folded in her lap. The Princes in the Tower and Cherry Ripe. The second is reproduced by the hundred thousand in a magazine and hangs in more British houses than any other picture of the century. He is painting for the print trade now, and the print trade takes everything he sends it.
suggested_refs: The Princes in the Tower (1878), Royal Holloway
Cherry Ripe (1879), reproduced as a Graphic Christmas supplement

stops.name: Birmingham, the chair of the provincial society
stops.date_confidence: the source dates the presidency 1881 to 1882
stops.campa: He takes the presidency of the Royal Birmingham Society of Artists, an office in the manufacturing city where the second Pre-Raphaelite generation was bred: Edward Burne-Jones is a Birmingham man, and the circle he and William Morris swore themselves into at Oxford called itself the Birmingham set. Millais holds the chair for two years. What the society wants from him is the Academy's authority attached to a New Street address, and he lends it without argument.
suggested_refs: The Royal Birmingham Society of Artists, New Street, Birmingham

stops.name: Saint Ouen, the island written into the patent
stops.date_confidence: attested month and year; the day is not given by the source
stops.campa: Queen Victoria makes him a baronet, the first painter in England to be given a hereditary title. The patent styles him of Palace Gate in Kensington and of Saint Ouen in the island of Jersey: the London house he built and the parish his father's family came from, joined in a single line of a royal warrant. Fifty-six years after the accident of a Southampton birth, the island of his childhood is written back into his name, and the title descends to his sons after him.
suggested_refs: The parish of Saint Ouen, Jersey, named in the 1885 baronetcy

stops.name: Palace Gate, the boy and the bubble
stops.date_confidence: attested year
stops.campa: He paints his grandson Willie James, five years old, in a green chair with a bowl of soapy water, looking up at a bubble that is about to be gone. The picture is sold, passes to A. and F. Pears, and is printed with a bar of soap added at the boy's feet on hoardings the length of the country. The copyright travels with the canvas. The most reproduced English picture of the century is a soap advertisement, and the child in it is his own daughter's son, painted in the Kensington studio.
suggested_refs: Bubbles (1886), Lady Lever Art Gallery, and the Pears soap advertisement made from it

segments.name: The Presidency, the Crypt, and the Statue

stops.name: Burlington House, elected President
stops.date_confidence: attested year; the month is inferred from Leighton's death in January 1896
stops.campa: Frederic Leighton dies in the January and the Academy elects Millais to the chair. He is sixty-six and already ill, his throat troubling him for a year. He takes the presidency at Burlington House, where the Academy moved in 1868, of the institution he entered as a child of eleven at Trafalgar Square and wrote a programme against at nineteen. Three years earlier Edward Burne-Jones resigned his associateship of the same body, having shown at the Grosvenor instead. Millais never left it for anywhere.
stops.quote: I doubt very much whether any man ever gets the credit of being quite square and above-board about his life and work.
stops.quote_source: Millais to his son on the eve of his election as President, in J. G. Millais, Life and Letters, vol. 1, p. 53
suggested_refs: Burlington House, Piccadilly, the Royal Academy's home since 1868
sources: J. G. Millais, Life and Letters, vol. 1, p. 53

stops.name: 2 Palace Gate, the last summer
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Cancer of the throat takes his voice before it takes him. In the last months at Palace Gate he talks to his son about the founding at Gower Street, and denies flatly and repeatedly that Rossetti had anything to do with what he painted. He dies on the thirteenth of August, sixty-seven years old, President of the Royal Academy for six months. The son writes the conversations down and publishes them three years later, and the denial goes into the record in the dying man's own words.
stops.quote: All nonsense! My pictures would have been exactly the same if I had never seen or heard of Rossetti.
stops.quote_source: Millais to his son, 1896, in J. G. Millais, Life and Letters, vol. 1, p. 54
suggested_refs: 2 Palace Gate, Kensington, where Millais died on 13 August 1896
sources: J. G. Millais, Life and Letters, vol. 1, p. 54

stops.name: St Paul's Cathedral, the crypt
stops.date_confidence: the source gives August 1896; the day is inferred
stops.campa: He is carried into the crypt of St Paul's and laid among the painters, in the ground that holds Reynolds and Turner and Lawrence. Forty-six years earlier the newspapers of this city called the same hand's work disgusting, revolting, and mean; the pall is now carried for a President of the Royal Academy. Jersey does not get him back and neither does Perthshire. He is put down in the floor of the national cathedral, in the city where he was made, and the exact bay of the grave is not recorded in anything reachable.
suggested_refs: The painters' corner of the St Paul's crypt: Reynolds, Turner, Lawrence, Millais

stops.name: Kinnoull, the grave above the Tay
stops.date_confidence: Effie Gray's burial at Kinnoull is attested; the date given here is her death and is reconstruction, the sources consulted giving no burial date
stops.campa: In the churchyard at Kinnoull above the Tay, where he painted the gravestones of The Vale of Rest and where her father's window lights the church, Effie lies under a marker she shares with their son George, dead at twenty-one. She married Ruskin in the house on the hill and Millais in the same house seven years afterward, and her own letters are printed only once she is past being asked about them. Her husband is in the crypt of St Paul's, four hundred miles to the south.
suggested_refs: The shared grave marker of Effie Gray and George Gray Millais, Kinnoull churchyard, Perth

stops.name: Millbank, Brock's bronze at the garden entrance
stops.date_confidence: attested year; month and day not given by the source
stops.campa: A memorial committee under the Prince of Wales, later Edward VII, commissions Thomas Brock, and the bronze goes up at the garden entrance of the new gallery at Millbank: Millais standing with palette and brushes, coat open, in the attitude people remembered him in. The Pall Mall Gazette calls it breezy. It faces the river a mile downstream from the Academy that made him and a mile upstream from the cathedral that holds him, and for forty-eight years nobody in the building behind it objects.
stops.quote: a breezy statue, representing the man in the characteristic attitude in which we all knew him
stops.quote_source: Pall Mall Gazette on Thomas Brock's statue, quoted in Wikipedia, John Everett Millais
suggested_refs: Thomas Brock's bronze of Millais, installed at the Tate Gallery in 1905

stops.name: Millbank, the gallery tries to be rid of him
stops.date_confidence: attested years 1953 and 1962 for the removal attempts, 1996 for the transfer, 2000 for the relocation; the stop takes the first
stops.campa: The gallery's own director wants the statue gone. Norman Reid tries in 1953, and again in 1962, to have it taken away, calling its presence positively harmful and proposing a Rodin for the spot. It stays. Ownership passes from the Ministry of Works to English Heritage in 1996 and then to the gallery itself, and in 2000 a later director moves the bronze from the main entrance round to the side of the building. The bronze now faces a side street, and visitors reach it only by walking past the door.
stops.quote_source: Norman Reid, director of the Tate Gallery, on the Millais statue, quoted in Wikipedia, John Everett Millais
suggested_refs: The Millais statue in its present position at the side of Tate Britain

stops.name: Tate Britain, the retrospective
stops.date_confidence: attested year; the opening month is not given by the source
stops.campa: A full retrospective opens at Millbank, and 151,000 people come to it in London before it travels to the Van Gogh Museum in Amsterdam and on to Fukuoka and Tokyo, more than 660,000 in all. What hangs together in those rooms is the carpenter's shop, the drowned girl in the Hogsmill water, the rock at Glenfinlas, the Perthshire flood, the boy with the soap. The century that moved his statue round the corner of the building queues at the door of it.
suggested_refs: Millais, Tate Britain, 2007, and its tour to Amsterdam, Fukuoka and Tokyo
